questions.text: The OLS estimator is β̂ = (X'X)⁻¹X'y. What is the condition required for this formula to exist?
options: The response y must be normally distributed
The matrix X'X must be invertible (no perfect multicollinearity among predictors)
The sample size n must exceed the number of predictors p by at least 100
questions.explanation: The formula requires (X'X)⁻¹ to exist, which requires X'X to be invertible (full rank). This fails when two or more columns of X are perfectly linearly dependent — perfect multicollinearity. In that case, there are infinitely many β vectors that minimise RSS, and the unique OLS solution does not exist.

questions.text: In the summary() output of lm(), the t-value for a coefficient is computed as: t = Estimate / Std. Error.
questions.explanation: The t-statistic tests H₀: βⱼ = 0. It equals the estimated coefficient divided by its standard error. Under H₀ and assuming normal errors, this statistic follows a t-distribution with n − p − 1 degrees of freedom.

questions.text: You fit lm(log(price) ~ log(carat)) on diamonds and get a slope of 1.676. How do you interpret this?
options: A 1-unit increase in carat is associated with a $1.676 increase in price
A 1% increase in carat is associated with a 1.676% increase in price
A 1-unit increase in log(carat) is associated with a $1.676 increase in price
The model explains 1.676% of the variance in price
questions.explanation: In a log-log model, the slope is the elasticity: a 1% increase in the predictor is associated with a (slope)% increase in the response. This follows from differentiating log(y) = β₀ + β₁log(x), which gives d(log y)/d(log x) = β₁, i.e., the percentage change in y per percentage change in x.

questions.text: The R² of the linear model lm(price ~ carat) is 0.849, while the log-log model lm(log(price) ~ log(carat)) gives R² = 0.933 (on log-price). Can we directly conclude the log-log model is better?
options: Yes — higher R² always means better model
Not directly, because the R² values are on different scales (raw price vs log price). We should also use residual diagnostics and compare within-scale metrics.
No — R² of 0.849 is already very high and further improvement is unnecessary
Yes, because R² closer to 1 is always the goal regardless of scale
questions.explanation: The two R² values are on different response scales (price vs log-price) and cannot be directly compared numerically. However, residual plots confirm that the log-log model has more constant variance and more symmetric residuals — two additional lines of evidence supporting the log-log model beyond the R² comparison.

questions.text: Why does lm() use QR decomposition rather than directly computing (X'X)⁻¹?
options: QR decomposition is slower but always produces integer-valued coefficients
Computing (X'X)⁻¹ directly can be numerically unstable when columns of X are nearly collinear; QR avoids inverting the matrix and is more stable
R cannot compute matrix inverses, so QR is used instead
questions.explanation: Inverting X'X amplifies numerical rounding errors, especially when the matrix is nearly singular (near-collinearity). QR decomposition avoids inversion entirely by reducing the normal equations to a triangular system (Rβ = Q'y) solved by back-substitution, which is both faster and more numerically stable.

questions.text: The F-statistic in summary(lm_fit) tests whether all slope coefficients are simultaneously equal to zero.
questions.explanation: The F-test compares the full model to the null model (intercept only). Under H₀: β₁ = β₂ = ... = βₚ = 0, the statistic F = [(TSS − RSS)/p] / [RSS/(n−p−1)] follows an F(p, n−p−1) distribution. A large F (small p-value) means at least one predictor has a non-zero coefficient.
